summary: Proposes a mechanism for dual stack hosts called Bump-in-the-Stack, which lets existing IPv4 applications work with IPv6 networks. It is an informational memo, and it was replaced by RFC 6535.

plainLanguage.summary: A little helper inside the computer rewrites old-style messages into new-style ones so older programs keep working.

questions: what is bump in the stack
how do ipv4 apps work on ipv6
subtitle: Let IPv4 applications talk to IPv6 networks transparently during the IPv4-to-IPv6 transition

tldr.problem: During the transition from IPv4 to IPv6, existing applications are IPv4-only. Writing new IPv6 applications takes time, but users need to access both IPv4 and IPv6 services immediately.
tldr.mechanism: The Bump-in-the-Stack technique inserts three modules into the host's networking stack: a translator (converts IPv4 packets to IPv6 and vice versa), an extension name resolver (intercepts DNS lookups and provides IPv4 addresses for IPv6 targets), and an address mapper (maps IPv4 addresses to IPv6 addresses).
tldr.outcome: Hosts can appear as dual stack (supporting both IPv4 and IPv6) without needing new applications. IPv4 apps can seamlessly communicate with IPv6 hosts. This was replaced by RFC 6535.

today: RFC 2767 is Informational and was obsoleted by RFC 6535, which provides updated guidance on this technique.

sections.title: The Transition Problem
sections.content:
IPv6 is the next generation of the Internet Protocol, addressing the exhaustion of IPv4 addresses. However, during the early transition phase, IPv6 applications are scarce compared to the thousands of mature IPv4 applications. Users and administrators need a way to access both IPv4 and IPv6 services without waiting for all applications to be rewritten.

RFC 1933 defines dual stack hosts, which implement both IPv4 and IPv6 completely. However, they require IPv6 versions of all needed applications. The Bump-in-the-Stack (BIS) technique, borrowed from IP security, offers an alternative: existing IPv4 applications can transparently communicate with IPv6 hosts through translation in the TCP/IP stack.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 is the new Internet. We can't instantly rewrite every program to use it, but we can build a translator inside the computer so old programs work anyway.

sections.title: The Three Components
sections.content:
A Bump-in-the-Stack host contains three modules inserted between the IPv4 applications and network drivers:

The Translator: Converts IPv4 packets to IPv6 packets and vice versa using the IP conversion mechanism (similar to SIIT, Stateless IP/ICMP Translator). When an IPv4 application sends a packet, the translator converts the IPv4 header to IPv6, then fragments the result if necessary (since IPv6 headers are typically 20 bytes larger than IPv4 headers). For incoming IPv6 packets, it reverses the process.

The Extension Name Resolver: Intercepts DNS lookups from IPv4 applications. When an application requests the 'A' record (IPv4 address) for a host, the resolver secretly queries for both 'A' and 'AAAA' records (IPv6 addresses). If only an 'AAAA' record exists, the resolver asks the address mapper to assign an IPv4 address, then returns the fake IPv4 address to the application.

The Address Mapper: Maintains a pool of IPv4 addresses (typically private addresses from RFC 1918) and a mapping table of IPv4 ↔ IPv6 address pairs. When asked to map an IPv6 address, it selects an unused IPv4 address from the pool and registers the pairing dynamically. The mapper also pre-registers the host's own addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Inside the stack are three workers. The translator changes packet headers. The resolver intercepts and modifies DNS answers. The mapper keeps a secret notebook of which fake IPv4 addresses correspond to real IPv6 addresses.

sections.title: How Communication Works
sections.content:
When the BIS host initiates: An IPv4 application requests the address for an IPv6 host. The extension resolver intercepts the DNS query, adds an AAAA record query, and gets back only an AAAA record. The resolver asks the mapper for an IPv4 address corresponding to the IPv6 address, receives one, creates an 'A' record for it, and returns it to the application. The application sends an IPv4 packet; the translator looks up the mapping for both source and destination addresses, converts the packet to IPv6, fragments if needed, and sends it. The IPv6 host replies with IPv6 packets; the translator converts them back to IPv4 and delivers them to the application.

When the IPv6 host initiates: The IPv6 host resolves the AAAA record for the BIS host (which was pre-registered) and sends an IPv6 packet to it. The translator receives it and looks up the mapping for the destination IPv6 address (finding the BIS host's own address) but not the source. The mapper assigns a new IPv4 address for the source, the translator converts the packet, and it reaches the IPv4 application. The application replies; the translator converts the reply to IPv6 and sends it back.
sections.plainLanguage: When your program talks first, the helper whispers to the name server to find the hidden IPv6 address, makes up a fake IPv4 address for it, and uses that behind the scenes. When someone else talks to you, the helper converts their message to IPv4 so your program understands it.

sections.title: What It Cannot Do
sections.content:
The Bump-in-the-Stack technique has important limitations. It works only for unicast communication (one-to-one); multicast (one-to-many) is not supported and requires a separate mechanism.

Since IPv4 options cannot be translated to IPv6 options, applications using IPv4 options will not work correctly. Similarly, most IPv6 option headers cannot be translated back to IPv4 (except fragment headers and routing headers), so incoming IPv6 packets with option headers may be rejected.

Many applications embed IP addresses in their protocol data—FTP is a classic example. When the mapper translates addresses in packet headers, it cannot translate embedded addresses in the application data itself. Thus, applications that send IP addresses as data will not work correctly through BIS.

When data is encrypted using IP addresses as keys, or when protocol data containing IP addresses is encrypted, BIS cannot translate the encrypted payload. Additionally, BIS cannot work with secure DNS (DNSSEC) since the extension name resolver cannot handle that protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: It only works for one-to-one conversations, not group chats. Programs that send IP addresses inside their messages, or programs that encrypt things using IP addresses, won't work. Encrypted DNS won't work either.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
When communicating with IPv4 hosts using IPv4 applications via BIS, security works normally for all network layers. Likewise, when the host uses native IPv6 applications to talk to IPv6 hosts, full security applies.

However, when IPv4 applications talk to IPv6 hosts through BIS, security above the network layer is compromised. If encrypted data contains or uses IP addresses as keys, BIS cannot translate it, breaking the communication. Therefore, users should upgrade applications to native IPv6 versions when security-above-network-layer is required for IPv6 communication.

Internally assigned IPv4 addresses never leave the host, so they do not negatively affect other hosts. The address pool can be exhausted if the host communicates with many IPv6 hosts without freeing old mappings, so the mapper should reuse the oldest unused addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: When your program talks to another IPv4 program, security is normal. When using a real IPv6 program, security is normal. But when an old IPv4 program talks through the translator to IPv6, some security features break. Upgrading the program is the right fix.
